42: Looking back upon your travels, you are %s.
44: the King himself seeks your counsel on the affairs of the Indies.
your word is heeded in the halls of power.
lords and bishops wait upon your pleasure at every levee.
45: you rule in His Majesty's name, and the planters doff their hats whenever your carriage passes by.
you hold court each evening and hang a pirate now and then for form's sake.
the colonists grumble at your taxes but toast your health.
46: you keep a great house and a pack of hounds.
your table is the finest for a hundred leagues.
you dine off silver plate and your tenants call you a fair master.
47: your fields stretch further than the eye can see.
you ride out each morning over your acres and count yourself well content.
the parish makes you churchwarden, and none dares remind you of your past.
48: you sit in judgement on rogues no worse than you were once yourself.
you are known for stern sentences and a soft heart.
you send many a smuggler to the stocks, and wink at a few old shipmates.
49: your ships carry sugar and hides to every port in Europe.
the counting-house hums with your affairs.
you lend money to governors and are paid in favours, which suit you better.
50: your tobacco fetches the best price on the quay.
you sit on your veranda each evening and watch the sea.
your harvests are the envy of your neighbours, and your rum is famed.
51: half the captains in port owe you money, and know it.
you lend gold at a fair rate, or so you assure your clients.
your strongroom holds more doubloons than you ever took at sea.
52: no ship drops anchor without your leave.
you collect the harbour dues and tell tall tales of your voyages to every new arrival.
you watch the ships come and go, and wish yourself aboard each one.
53: your three sloops ply the coast and bring home a fair profit.
you send other men to sea now, and keep the better share for yourself.
your ships sail and your purse grows.
54: the mill turns and the sugar flows from dawn to dusk.
your cane grows tall and your account books grow fat.
the heat and the flies plague you, but the sugar pays for all.
55: you sell cloth and candles at a modest profit.
your shop is well known and your scales mostly honest.
you haggle over every penny with the zeal you once spent on Spanish galleons.
56: you build stout sloops for men as reckless as you once were.
the smell of pitch and sawdust stays with you.
you mend the hulls of other men's prizes and keep your counsel.
57: you grow yams and keep a few goats.
you plough a small field and pray each year for rain.
your hands are rough and your conscience easy.
58: you pour rum for sailors and sell rumours to any captain with coin.
your stories grow taller with every jug you pour.
you keep a cutlass behind the bar and a parrot on the shelf.
59: you mend your nets and watch the sails go by.
the sea still feeds you, if only on a little fish.
you row out each dawn in a leaky boat, and when a galleon passes far off, you sigh.
60: you haul ropes for a captain half your age.
you swab decks and keep your past to yourself.
you sail under another man's orders and grumble at every watch.
61: you carry other men's cargo up the quay and dream of the gold you once had.
your back aches each night from barrels of salt pork.
you load the very ships you once would have taken as prizes.
62: you scrub pots in a tavern kitchen for your bread.
you fetch and carry for a merchant who never once asks your name.
no one remembers the captain you once were.
63: you wander from town to town with a sack on your back.
you sleep under the stars and sing old sea songs for a crust.
64: you live on the charity of the church.
you sleep in a doorway and dream of gold.
you sit on the quay in rags, telling tales of treasure that no one believes.
65: you beg for coppers from the sailors who once feared your name.
you hold out your hat to strangers on the quay.
you beg at the church door and children mock your tales of glory.
66: you rot in a cell and curse the day you first went to sea.
the gaoler is your only company.
you count the days in chains, and the rats are your only shipmates.
67: your name is soon forgotten, as if you had never sailed at all.
no one marks your passing, and the sea keeps your secrets.
the wind blows over an unmarked grave, and the world forgets you.
